posts.title: What Is Epistemic Injustice in Autism? Why Lived Experience Must Lead the Conversation on Autistic Mental Health
posts.excerpt: Why We Hold the Autistic Mental Health Conference; Lived Experience, Professional Knowledge, and the Fight Against Epistemic Injustice
posts.text:
There is a question we return to every time we begin planning the Autistic Mental Health Conference: why does this need to exist? Because the answer matters so much that it bears repeating; loudly, and often.

The truth is, Autistic people have long been spoken about rather than spoken with. Our mental health, our distress, our needs, and our potential have been catalogued, theorised, and debated; frequently by people who have never lived a single day inside a neurodivergent mind. The result is a body of knowledge that is, at best, incomplete, and at worst, actively harmful.

The Problem With Knowledge That Excludes Us

In philosophy, there is a concept called epistemic injustice ; a term coined by Miranda Fricker to describe the harms that occur when someone is wronged specifically in their capacity as a knower. As someone whose testimony is dismissed, whose perspective is not taken seriously, whose understanding of their own experience is treated as less valid than an outside observer’s interpretation of it. Autistic people experience epistemic injustice constantly.

We are told that we lack insight into our own minds, that our self-reports are unreliable and that professionals, however well-meaning, know our experience better than we do. We are diagnosed using frameworks built without our input, treated using therapies we were never consulted on, and supported by systems that were designed around assumptions about us rather than actual understanding of us.

The consequences are not abstract; misdiagnosis, missed diagnosis, inappropriate treatment, iatrogenic harm, burnout, and crisis. These are the real-world outcomes of a knowledge system that has historically excluded the very people it claims to serve. When our testimony is discredited, we are not merely overlooked. We are harmed.

Lived Experience Is Not A Supplement: It Is The Foundation

There is a tendency, even in progressive spaces, to treat lived experience as a nice addition to professional knowledge. A human interest story to open the presentation, a quote to add warmth to a report, a token “service user perspective” at the end of a panel of experts. We reject that model entirely.

Lived experience is not anecdote, nor an emotion in place of evidence. It is a distinct and irreplaceable form of knowledge; one that professional training, however rigorous, cannot replicate. An Autistic person who has navigated a mental health crisis, survived a system that failed to understand them, and developed their own frameworks for making sense of their experience carries knowledge that no textbook can contain.

At the same time, we do not dismiss professional and academic knowledge. Research, clinical understanding, and systemic analysis all have vital roles to play. The problem has never been that professional knowledge exists, the problem is the hierarchy; the assumption that it sits above lived experience rather than alongside it.

The Autistic Mental Health Conference is built on a different premise; that genuine understanding of Autistic mental health requires both , in genuine dialogue, with neither elevated above the other.

What Happens When Both Come Together

When professional knowledge and lived experience meet as equals, something powerful happens. Research findings become grounded in human reality, clinical frameworks are tested against the people they are meant to describe, lived experience narratives gain language and context that help them travel further; into policy, into practice, into the spaces where decisions are made.

Speakers bring decades of academic and theoretical work on neurodiversity, challenging the deficit-based frameworks that have dominated the field. Other speakers bring personal insight into the lived mechanics of masking; what it costs, how it develops, and what reducing it actually requires in practice. Some present work that sits at the exact intersection of the two; rigorous, co-produced, and rooted simultaneously in research and in Autistic life. These conversations are the beginnings of a more equitable structure in society, they model what it looks like when the people most affected by a body of knowledge are also among those generating it.

Conferences As Sites Of Epistemic Repair

Epistemic injustice cannot be undone by a single event, but conferences, when designed with intention, can be sites of something we might call epistemic repair. When we build a platform that centres neurodivergent speakers, we are making a structural argument; that these voices belong at the front of the room, not the margins. We are creating the conditions for Autistic people to be heard as knowers; as people with genuine expertise in their own lives and in the broader landscape of neurodivergent experience.

When we gather a community of Autistic individuals, parents, professionals, and allies under a shared theme (this year, “Ecosystemic Causes of Mental Health Issues” ) we are collectively interrogating the systems that shape our wellbeing. We are naming the environmental and structural causes of distress rather than locating the problem within Autistic people themselves. That reframing is, in itself, an act of epistemic justice.

When attendees leave, whether they are Autistic individuals with new language for their own experience, professionals with a more accurate and humane understanding of the people they support, or researchers whose thinking has been genuinely challenged; the knowledge generated at this conference travels outward into the world.

Why This Conference, Why Now

Autistic mental health remains one of the most urgent and underserved areas of both research and care. Autistic people face significantly elevated rates of mental helth struggles, suicidality, and burnout, and the systems meant to support us frequently compound rather than alleviate these challenges.

The 2026 Autistic Mental Health Conference is our answer to that reality; a meaningful, community-rooted one, built on the conviction that when Autistic people are able to share knowledge, receive knowledge, and be recognised as legitimate contributors to the conversation about their own lives, something shifts. Knowledge becomes more accurate, care becomes more humane, community becomes possible. That is why we hold this conference.

That is why we hope you will join us.

posts.title: Welcome to NeuroHub Community
posts.excerpt: There are a lot of organisations that claim to support neurodivergent people. There are far fewer that are actually built by us, for us; grounded in our own lived experience, our own understanding of what it means to navigate a world that was never designed with us in mind. NeuroHub Community is different. We were […]
posts.text:
There are a lot of organisations that claim to support neurodivergent people. There are far fewer that are actually built by us, for us; grounded in our own lived experience, our own understanding of what it means to navigate a world that was never designed with us in mind.

NeuroHub Community is different. We were founded in January 2026 with a clear purpose:

To create a genuinely neurodivergent-led space where Autistic and neurodivergent people, families, and professionals can access support that respects who they are.

Who We Are

NeuroHub is a neurodiversity consultancy, training, and community organisation based in the UK. Everything we do is shaped by neurodivergent-led values; identity-first, rights-based, and rooted in the understanding that distress is contextual, not pathological. We do not view neurodivergent people as problems to be fixed. We view systems, environments, and relationships as things that can be changed.

We work with neurodivergent adults directly, and we also offer bespoke mentoring and consultation for families who want to better understand and support their neurodivergent loved ones. Whether you are Autistic, ADHD, or otherwise neurodivergent, whether you are newly identified or have known for years; there is a place for you here.

What We Offer

Consultancy and Mentoring for Individuals

If you are looking for one-to-one support tailored to your life, our individual consultancy services offer a space to explore your identity, your challenges, and your goals without judgement. We also work with families seeking guidance on how to support a neurodivergent person in their lives.

Explore individual consultancy →

Mindfulness Meditations

We have developed a growing library of mindfulness meditations designed specifically with neurodivergent nervous systems in mind; not the sanitised, one-size-fits-all approach that rarely works for us, but something that actually meets you where you are.

Access our mindfulness meditations →

Supporting Autistic People Course

Our flagship training course introduces the Six-Point Framework; a practical, values-driven approach to understanding and supporting Autistic people. Whether you are a professional, a family member, or an Autistic person wanting to better understand your own experience, this course offers genuine insight rather than deficit-based narratives.

Explore the Supporting Autistic People course →

Re-Storying Autism Video Course & eBook

Most of us have grown up surrounded by stories about Autism that were not written by Autistic people. Stories that frame us through deficit, difficulty, and disorder. Re-Storying Autism invites you to set those narratives aside and build something more honest in their place.

This on-demand video course and workbook (developed from NeuroHub’s Six-Point Framework) takes learners through seven pre-recorded lessons covering identity and language, sensory and emotional landscapes, Autistic play and learning, burnout, trauma, and the wisdom held within Autistic community. It also includes a full eBook to accompany the course.

Whether you are a professional, a family member, or an Autistic person who wants to extend to yourself the same compassion you offer others; this course was made for you.

Currently available at a permanently reduced price of £39.99.

Explore Re-Storying Autism →

The NeuroHub Community Space

Our community platform is where neurodivergent people come together; to share, to learn, to be seen. This is not a support group built on pity; it is a space built on solidarity. We would love to have you with us.

Join the NeuroHub Community →

Professional Gateway

For professionals working alongside neurodivergent people (whether in healthcare, education, social care, or beyond) the Professional Gateway offers access to neurodivergent-led training, resources, and community. Because good practice starts with listening to neurodivergent voices.

Explore the Professional Gateway →

2026 Autistic Mental Health Conference

The 2nd Annual Autistic Mental Health Conference takes place 14–16 August 2026, running as a hybrid event with in-person sessions in Brighton. This is a space for Autistic people, allies, and professionals to come together and meaningfully engage with the intersection of Autism and mental health; from a perspective that centres Autistic voices and lived experience.

Find out more and register →

Our Ethos

We believe that neurodivergent people deserve more than tolerance. We believe in genuine inclusion; which means changing systems, not people. Our work draws on the double empathy problem, monotropism, neuroqueer theory, and an ecosystemic understanding of distress. In practice, this means we will never ask you to mask, comply, or perform neurotypicality in order to receive support.

We are not here to make you more palatable to a world that should already be making room for you. We are here to walk alongside you as you figure out what a good life actually looks like on your own terms.

If any of what you have read resonates, we would love to connect. Explore our services, join the community, or reach out directly. NeuroHub is here — and it was built with you in mind.

posts.title: Embracing Our Autistic Selves: Knowing The Autistic Bodymind
posts.excerpt: The following is drawn from Session 4 of the Embracing Our Autistic Selves course, on the autistic bodymind, sensory knowledge, interoception, and burnout. We live in a culture that has spent decades separating the body from the mind. Medicine treats the body, psychiatry treats the mind, and Autistic people, who experience both as inseparably entangled, […]
posts.text:
The following is drawn from Session 4 of the Embracing Our Autistic Selves course, on the autistic bodymind, sensory knowledge, interoception, and burnout.

We live in a culture that has spent decades separating the body from the mind. Medicine treats the body, psychiatry treats the mind, and Autistic people, who experience both as inseparably entangled, get caught in the gap between them, told their sensory responses are symptoms, their fatigue is attitude, their dysregulation is a behaviour problem; it is none of those things.

The bodymind is a description of how we actually work, not a metaphor. The body and mind are not two systems running in parallel; they are one integrated system, in constant communication, constantly giving us information about the world we’re moving through. For Autistic people, that system works differently, not worse, differently .

Understanding that difference is, I would argue, one of the most important things we can do for ourselves.

Sensory Experience Is Knowledge, Not Pathology

Before any words are spoken, before any explanation is offered, your sensory world is already telling you things. Whether a space is safe, or if a person can be trusted, it might also tell us whether a situation is going to cost you more than is sustainable.

I know almost immediately if I can cope with a space. Wide-open spaces with lots of people; I know that’s going to be a struggle. Someone speaking at length about things my brain can’t compute, the same. A friend’s living room, a conversation about something I care deeply about, books around me? These are all sensory experiences that give me information; that is intelligence, not disorder.

When our sensory responses are treated as symptoms, what gets lost is the signal. Dysregulation is not manipulation, and it is not a behaviour problem.; it is a communication. Something is off-kilter, something is unmet. The appropriate response to a signal is curiosity, not correction.

This matters enormously in education, in healthcare, in workplaces. If someone is dysregulated, the question is not how to stop the dysregulation, rather it is:

What is this telling us about the environment?

Alexithymia And The Language Gap

A lot of us are alexithymic; alexithymia is the difficulty identifying and interpreting our own emotional states. Research puts it at around 50% of Autistic people, though I suspect the real figure is higher, and I also suspect it’s not always a fixed trait. Like most aspects of Autistic experience, it fluctuates, and interacts with stress, trauma, and overwhelm.

For me, anything that raises my heart rate can feel like anxiety. Exercise, excitement, actual anxiety; they all feel the same. Trying to work out which is which is genuinely hard work, and I’ve talked to so many Autistic people who describe themselves as emotionless, only for it to become clear very quickly that they’re not emotionless at all. They experience emotions, they just can’t always interpret them. The language they’ve been given doesn’t match the experiences they’re having.

This is a mismatch; between an Autistic neurocognitive system and a neurotypical emotional vocabulary.

Trauma compounds this. For many of us, lived experience of trauma teaches the bodymind to create distance between Self and experience. It becomes a survival mechanism; putting space between yourself and the things happening to you, that distance, over time, can become the default.

Meerkatting And Monotropic Demand Avoidance

Tanya Adkin’s concept of meerkat mode captures this nicely. It’s that desperate, hypervigilant state where you’re scanning constantly for the thing that will hook you in, give you that monotropic flow that will regulate you; but you’re looking for it in the wrong places, because by the time you’re meerkatting, you often don’t realise you’re doing it. It can look manic, it can feel urgent; it is the point just before the spiral, the moment before the rabbit hole opens up.

There’s also something worth saying about demand avoidance in this context. When we’re burned out, when we’re overwhelmed, the very signals from our body “ you need to rest, you need to eat, you need to sleep ” can start to feel like demands. If our bodyminds are already at capacity, those signals can get avoided alongside everything else. The result is what many of us know well; realising at 3pm that we haven’t eaten in 24 hours, or getting into bed and only then noticing the pain we’ve been carrying all day.

The Autistic bodymind under pressure behaves a bit like hypovolaemic shock; redirecting processing to what it has decided are the essential things, switching off channels to cope, much like a circulatory system redicrecting bloodflow in cases of blood loss. The problem is that the brain is not always right about what’s essential, and a lot of what gets switched off is more essential than we realise.

The Cost Of Conflict

When the sensory system is overwhelmed and we’re expected to perform as normal, when the body is going through the motions of functioning whilst the mind is in a state of overwhelm and desperation; that conflict is the costly part of masking. It is operating outside of what is sustainable. That conflict deserves to be noticed, bookmarked, and not pathologised; instead recognised as information: what I am doing right now is not sustainable .

This is where unhealthy coping mechanisms come in. Rumination, which in a monotropic mind isn’t just thinking about something, it’s thinking about it in ultra-high definition. Substance use, avoidance, hese things are attempts to manage an experience that has become unmanageable.

The question worth sitting with is: what boundaries do we need to set to reduce our exposure to those unsustainable situations? Not because we can eliminate them (we live in a world that is fundamentally not built for us) but because we can minimise them. This answer will look different for each of us.

Burnout Doesn’t Always Arrive Gradually

One of the things that came up in this session, and that I hear consistently from Autistic people, is that burnout doesn’t always announce itself. There’s no gentle slope; you’re in meerkat mode, hypervigilant, constantly on, scanning and seeking, and then you’re not. Suddenly you’re in it, crashed out, unable to leave the bed, unable to talk. The foggy, thick perspex between you and the world that some people describe; what feels to me like TV static. For many people, it’s others who notice the burnout before they do.

This is part of why checking in with ourselves matters. Knowing what our own early signals are and what our window of tolerance looks and feels like when we’re approaching its edges. Three check-ins across a day, just to locate yourself, it’s survival information/

Autistic burnout does not have a single profile. For me, it intersects with schizophrenia and tends to present as paranoia and anxiety, for others it looks like a depressive episode, for some it mirrors a hy

posts.title: Autism & How To Solve The NEET Problem
posts.excerpt: In recent dates the news in the united kingdom has been discussing how 25% of young people are not in education, employment, or training. This article presents an argument that the solution is to better support Autistic young people.
posts.text:
When you hear the term NEET’s you could be forgiven for not immediately realising that we are referring to human beings. The phrase could conjure images of illness or robotic workers, but it doesn’t sound particularly human. A NEET is government jargon in the UK for a young person who is ” Not in Education, Employment, or Training”.

For Autistic people, dehumanising language is something that is part of every day life. We are dehumanised, sometimes, multiple times a day, and in countless different ways. This highlights an important issue, because Autistic young people are far more likely to feel into the NEET criteria.

Autism And Employment

The Buckland Review Of Autism And Employment found that just 3 in 10 of Autistic people are in employment. This is compared to 5 in 10 of disabled people in. General and 8 in 10 of non-disabled people. It is clear that when compared to the general population, employment is a significant issue of marginalisation for Autistic people.

Comparing Autistic people to the non-disabled group, I used a simple contingency table to quite quickly establish that the odd ratio for Autistic people not being in employment is 9.33. In simple terms, Autistic people in the UK are just over 9 times more likely to be unemployed than non-disabled people.

Why Is This Relevant To The NEET Discussion?

If Autistic people are 9 times more likely to be unemployed in the UK, then it is reasonable to infer this rate will be similar among young people not in education, employment, or training. So, if you imagine people as marble in a bag, for every non-disabled marble in the NEET bag, we need to add 9 more Autistic marbles.

A quick Google search however demonstrates an inconsistency in the data from the Office For National Statistics . 8.7% of the NEET demographic are non-disabled, which is not all that surprising.

What is surprising is that only around 30% are disabled. Given that disabled people includes Autistic young people, and that Autistic young people here we assume are around 9 times more likely to be unemployed, I would expect this percentage to be a lot higher.

What Is Driving The Disparity?

O’Nions et al (2023) noted that there are approximately 463,500 diagnosed Autistic people in the UK and a potential number of 1.197 million undiagnosed. They also noted age disparities in diagnoses with around 1 in 250 5 to 9 year olds receiving a new diagnosis of autism, compared to only 1 in 4000 of 20 to 49 year olds.

It seems likely to mean that the missing disabled people in the NEET statistics are undiagnosed Autistic people. Undiagnosed Autistic people present an issue of unmet needs and poorer outcomes, meaning that a large portion of NEET demographic are likely to be Autistic people who are trying their best to simply stay alive, which in todays society, feels like a full time job itself.

What Does This Mean For Addressing The NEET Issue And Why Does It Matter?

If undiagnosed Autistic young people are, in fact, a large portions of the NEET population, then the following steps need to be taken in order to lower these statistics:

• Reform the SEND system into one that upholds student rights, creates meaningful and effective means of accessing education, and supports children and young people to access education within their ability to do so, and not how society feels they should.

• Reform UK mental health systems, and recognised that Autistic people are also over-represented in mental health settings which are largely unqualified and under-respourced to be supporting them.

• Make working from home a legal right in jobs that can be done so effectively for disabled young people and adults and not an accommodation we have to beg for.

• Reform and properly fund the NHS autism and ADHD referral pathways to improve diagnostic rates and the subsequent outcomes associated with them.

These points are important because this issue goes further than simply being unemployed. Autistic people are significantly more likely to die by suicide, be criminalised, and emerging research supports the long-held claim that we may be significantly at risk of Substance use issues and it’s outcomes.

All these issues are related to, and further compounded by, unemployment. Simply put, by failing young people early on, our consecutive governments have created a situation where a growing number of Autistic young people may be a risk of serious and significant harm. An outcome that, if it came from their parents, would have resulted in social services intervention.

It is clear that this is a critical issue that needs to be handled aggressively and at speed. Sadly, it is unlikely to be managed effectively in the near future, and so it falls to us, the community, to ensure that Autistic voices are heard.

posts.title: Emotional Flatness In Autism: Self-Preservation Through Disassociation
posts.excerpt: A common accusation that Autistic people face is one of emotional flatness, or having a flat affect. In more colloquial terms, Autistic people are accused of being emotionless. While Autistic people may often present what appears to be a limited or reduced range and/or depth of emotional responses, it is incorrect to assume this equates to a lack of emotional experience or landscape.
posts.text:
A common accusation that Autistic people face is one of emotional flatness, or having a flat affect. In more colloquial terms, Autistic people are accused of being emotionless. While Autistic people may often present what appears to be a limited or reduced range and/or depth of emotional responses, it is incorrect to assume this equates to a lack of emotional experience or landscape.

Autistic people, like any human, have rich and deeply textured inner lives, but for a number of reasons, do not present them in ways that neuronormative society deems an appropriate performance of emotional reaction.

This article will approach this matter from three lines of argument:

• Interoceptive and cultural differences resulting in alexithymia

• Self-preservation through disassociation from the emotional environment

• Emotional response as a performance of normative perceptions

1. Interoception, Culture, And Alexithymia

Autistic people are known for experiencing differences in their interoceptive sense. Interoception is the sense that tells us what is happening within our body. It is how we feel hunger, thirst, the need to use the toilet, and more importantly, the physiological changes associated with emotions.

The challenge is that if you are not able to as acutely identify those physiological changes, or differentiate them in a way that is meaningful for yourself, it becomes very difficult to identify and articulate those emotions in a way that can be communicated to others. This means that for Autistic people, we need extra time to process and define what we are feeling.

It’s important to note the cultural element involved here. Rather than immediately assuming that Autistic interoception is less accurate, we should consider the impact of neuronormative culture on how we interpret our emotions. There is a concept in linguistics called “Linguistic Relativity” (The Sapir-Whorf Hypothesis). Essentially, our use and understandig of language defines our reality.

For Autistic people growing and developing over their lifespan in a normative culture, the language we are provided with to understand and articulate our emotions does not provide an accurate reflection of the inner experience of our emotions. Thus, we may not present our emotions in the expected way because we are trying to communicate an experience for which normative culture does not provide adequate language or reality.

2. Self-Preservation Through Disassociation

Autistic people grow up in a world that is inherently unsafe and traumatic for us. It is, essentially, why we learn to mask. Masking is not a conscious deception, rather, it is a reflexive survival skill that is necessary in a world that penalises our difference. Sadly, this does not protect us from the negative emotional experience of this traumatic world.

Autistic people may display a limited range of emotions on the surface while experiencing a torrent of complex feelings within. This is because one of the easiest ways for us to cope with our intense emotions (that we may not even be able to identify) and still present a normatively safe presentation is to fragment the connection between our inner world and the perception of our visible affect. What looks like absence on the surface, is a reflexive containment of intensity underneath.

3. Emotion As Performance

Finally, we have to consider that normative emotional range demands performance over candor. Autistic feelings are filtered through neurotypical comfort, and so we are forced to perform whatever of the reactions available to us will be perceived as the most acceptable. The truth of the matter however, is that whichever option we go with, there is normally a professional or neurotypical accusing us of doing it wrong.

The concluding point to this article is this; accusing Autistic people of being emotionless or disengaged due to your perception of their outward affect constitutes a microagression at best, and normative violence at worst. It is a discriminatory assumption that far too many fall into the trap of inflicting upon Autistic bodyminds. Autistic people are not emotionless, they are trying to keep you comfortable.

posts.title: Embracing Our Autistic Selves: What Other Autistic People Teach Us
posts.excerpt: An exploration of Autistic identity through the conversations held in the “Embracing Out Autistic Selves” course at NeuroHub Community
posts.text:
On the relief of finding your people, the grief of finding them too late, and the quietly radical act of building identity together.
NeuroHub Community | Embracing Our Autistic Selves | Module 2 | Lesson 3

In the second module of our Embracing Our Autistic Selves course, we sat together and asked a deceptively simple question: what do you feel when you think about other autistic people? What followed was one of the most moving conversations I have had the privilege of being part of.

Relief. That was the first word offered. Then safety. Then straightforwardness; the luxury of not needing to explain yourself from the beginning. Then someone described the particular comfort of recognising, in another person, the same wavelength, and not having to perform the adjustment you carry everywhere else.

These weren’t academic answers. They were instinctive ones. The kind that emerge when you ask someone to describe something they’ve never quite had the words for before, and they reach for them anyway. And they told us something important: that for many of us, the experience of being around other autistic people isn’t just pleasant, it’s genuinely restorative in a way that other social experiences rarely are.

This post is an attempt to draw out the themes from that conversation, because I think they matter well beyond the room we were in.

The ADAR And The Feeling Of Being Found

Some of you will be familiar with the concept of the autistic radar; the ADAR. That phenomenon where you meet someone and something just clicks, before you can explain quite why. You know. And increasingly, looking back, so many of us can identify the people in our earlier lives who we now understand to have been autistic, even if neither of us had the language for it then.

For me, one person comes to mind clearly from childhood. At the time, I remember feeling something close to pity, the kind of response I had absorbed uncritically from the environment around me. He was always last to be picked for things. He stood apart, and I perceived the difference, embarrassingly, responding to it in the most normative way possible. Reflecting back over a decade of advocacy work, I feel something like guilt about that. And yet, I also think I have to let it go, because carrying shame about who we were before we knew better serves no real purpose. We learn, and then we do better. That’s what matters.

What that boy actually taught me (though I couldn’t have articulated it at the time) was something about being unapologetically yourself. Even when the world responds to that with confusion or exclusion, there is something quietly dignified about simply being what you are.

So many of us discover our Autistic selves through Autistic children; as if we are able to reparent ourselves, just a little, through what we learn from them.

This came up powerfully in our discussion; how many of us, as Autistic adults, first encountered autism clearly through a child. A son or daughter whose assessment process sent us down a rabbit hole of reading and recognition. A child we worked with professionally, in whose behaviour we saw something too familiar. In a previous generation, autism was so consistently framed through a normative lens that we could stand right next to it in our own families and never see it clearly. Now, with marginally more affirming frameworks available, we encounter Autistic children who are living, with difficulty and unevenly, in a world that at least sometimes names their experience. And in watching them, we find ourselves.

The Grief Of Finding Out Too Late

Not everyone finds out in time to have the conversation they needed to have.

Several people in our group described recognising autism retrospectively in parents, grandparents, and siblings, people who had shaped their lives profoundly, without either party having the words for what they shared. Post-it notes left on the kitchen counter instead of conversations. The same meal eaten every single night for years. A particular intensity, a particular kind of intelligence, a particular way of being in the world that made total sense once you knew what you were looking at; and broke your heart a little, once you did.

There is a specific kind of grief in this. Not just the loss of the person, but the loss of the conversation you never got to have. The years of miscommunication and distance and mutual incomprehension that might have been different (not necessarily easy, but different) if the language had existed earlier. If someone, somewhere along the line, had known what to look for.

One person described it as the feeling of years that have been lost, of alienation from family members who were, in a sense, your own people all along, and never knowing it. Another described looking back at a parent’s struggles with a completely different understanding now; seeing the outbursts not as inexplicable, but as sensory experiences without a framework. Seeing the self-medication not as weakness, but as what happens when someone spends a lifetime trying to manage a nervous system nobody helped them understand.

This is one of the most quietly devastating things about the previous generation’s relationship with autism: not just that they were undiagnosed, but that the absence of language meant that even the people closest to them couldn’t offer the right kind of understanding. And we, their Autistic children, internalised their struggles without understanding them. We promised ourselves we wouldn’t become them, and in doing so, we were often fighting the very thing that might have finally connected us.

Community spaces like this become places we seek out, perhaps because they act as a surrogate for the autism-affirming family that many of us needed growing up and are only now discovering through connection to others outside our blood families.

Not All Autistic People Are Our People; And That’s Okay

An important moment in our session came when we acknowledged something that can feel uncomfortable to say out loud: not every Autistic person is going to be safe for us, not every Autistic person is our neurokin.
“Neurokin” is a term that emerged partly as a decolonial replacement for “neurotribes”, a word that had been widely used after Steve Silberman’s important book of the same name, before Indigenous communities raised concerns about the cultural appropriation of the word “tribes”. Neurokin (your chosen neurodivergent family), the people you feel most fundamentally connected to, is what we were reaching for when we used that earlier term.

The honest truth is: not all Autistic people are that. Being Autistic doesn’t automatically make someone safe, any more than sharing any other identity characteristic guarantees alignment of values. We discussed what used to be called “Aspie supremacy”, the use of the Asperger’s label as a kind of social delineator, where people with significant internalised ableism would place themselves on one side of an imaginary line an

posts.title: Autism, Complex Mental Health, and the Right to Be Fully Human
posts.excerpt: Why complex needs are the rule rather than the exception in the Autistic community and how to support Autistic mental health.
posts.text:
There is a version of autism that gets talked about a lot, and it usually looks like a particular kind of struggle with social difficulties, sensory sensitivities, and a need for routine. It is sympathetic, fundable, and for the most part, considered safe to discuss in polite company.

Then there is the version that does not get talked about nearly enough. The Autistic person who has also developed a dependency on alcohol or drugs. The one who has experienced psychotic episodes. The one whose trauma has shaped into something clinicians label a personality disorder. This version makes people uncomfortable, and that discomfort, that turning away, is doing serious harm.

I want to talk about it directly, because this is not a niche issue. It is one of the defining, unspoken crises in Autistic mental health.

Why Autistic People Are Disproportionately Affected By Complex Mental Health Conditions

The research is increasingly clear: Autistic people experience mental health difficulties at significantly higher rates than the general population, but it isn’t just the rates that matter, it is the nature of those difficulties. Autism and mental health do not intersect in simple, clean-edged ways.

Studies consistently find that Autistic people have higher rates of anxiety and depression, but also of conditions that carry far more stigma; psychosis, post-traumatic stress disorder, eating disorders, and substance use disorders. These are the downstream effects of a society that was not built for us, and of a mental health system that still doesn’t know how to hold us.

The Role Of Trauma

To understand why complex mental health presentations are so common in Autistic communities, you have to understand how much cumulative trauma many of us carry. Autistic children are significantly more likely to experience bullying, social exclusion, physical and emotional abuse, and medical neglect. Many grow up in environments where their needs aren’t just unmet, they are actively pathologised. They are told there is something wrong with them before they have the language to push back, and they internalise those ideas, believing them to be true.

That kind of sustained, relational trauma shapes the nervous system; it shapes how we regulate emotion, how we interpret threat, how we relate to our own bodies. It creates the conditions from which psychosis, personality disorders, and addiction can grow.

The Consequences Of Masking

Masking (the practice of suppressing or concealing Autistic traits in order to pass as neurotypical) is exhausting, chronic, and corrosive. It is not a harmless coping strategy. Rather, a prolonged act of self-erasure that accumulates across years and decades. The mental health cost is enormous; high rates of Autistic burnout, dissociation, identity fragmentation, and a persistent sense that the person you present to the world is not really you.

For many Autistic people, substances become part of the masking toolkit long before addiction becomes visible. Alcohol reduces social anxiety; Cannabis dulls sensory overload; Stimulants help with executive function. The use is rarely recreational in the way it might be for a neurotypical peer, it is functional, adaptive, and deeply rational given the circumstances. That doesn’t make it safe, but it does mean we are framing it entirely wrong when we treat Autistic addiction as a moral failing rather than a survival response.

Delayed Diagnosis And Its Cost

The average age of Autistic diagnosis in the UK remains shockingly high, particularly for women, non-binary people, and people of colour. Many Autistic adults will have spent years or decades seeking help from mental health services for difficulties that were rooted in being unrecognised Autistic people in a world that made them suffer.

Those years matter; undiagnosed, unsupported, and misunderstood people develop coping mechanisms, some of which become problems in their own right. They receive diagnoses that fit the symptoms but miss the cause. They end up in mental health systems ill-equipped to see them whole. Their bodyminds are medicalised even though their mind is reacting adaptively to extreme duress.

How Stigma Compounds The Harm

Mental health stigma is not a uniform experience. There is a hierarchy to it, and Autistic people with complex needs often find themselves at the bottom.

Addiction carries stigma that other mental health conditions do not. It is still, in many professional and public contexts, treated as a choice (as a character flaw) rather than as a health condition with biological, psychological, and social roots. For Autistic people, this is especially damaging, because the pathway into addiction is so often a direct response to unmet need and unrecognised neurodivergence.

Psychosis is similarly stigmatised. The fear, the cultural othering, the way psychotic experiences are treated as fundamentally unknowable or frightening; this shuts down compassionate engagement before it can begin. Autistic people who experience psychosis frequently report being dismissed by services as “too complex” or bounced between mental health teams who cannot agree on a primary diagnosis.

Personality disorder diagnoses carry perhaps the heaviest stigma of all within clinical settings. They are often deployed (consciously or not) as a way of explaining away difficult behaviour rather than understanding its origins. For Autistic women in particular, complex-PTSD and emotionally unstable presentations have historically been misdiagnosed as personality disorders, with all the therapeutic nihilism that label can attract.

When a person’s distress is named as a disorder of character rather than a response to circumstances, we stop asking the most important question; what do you need?

This stigma does not only live in the general public. It lives in consulting rooms, multidisciplinary team meetings, and the policies that govern who gets access to specialist support. Autistic people with complex mental health needs are often told they are too Autistic for mental health services and too mentally unwell for autism services. They fall through the gap because no one has taken responsibility for bridging the gaps.

A Rights-Based Frame: Complex Needs Are Not Disqualifying

A rights-based approach to Autistic mental health insists on something simple but radical; having complex needs does not make you less deserving of care. It does not make your experiences less valid. It does not make you a lesser Autistic person.

Complexity is not a character flaw, it is, more often than not, the accumulated evidence of how hard a person has had to fight to survive in an ecosystem that was overtly hostile for them. Addiction, psychosis, trauma responses, these are not disqualifying conditions; they are part of the full picture of a human life, and they deserve the same compassion, curiosity, and clinical rigour as any other presentation.

The neurodivergent rights movement has rightly pushed bac

posts.title: Autism and Mental Health: The System Wasn’t Built for Us
posts.excerpt: What is the systemic relationship between autism and mental health? This article explores why Autistic people struggle to access services.
posts.text:
If you are Autistic or Neurodivergent and have tried to access mental health support, there is a real chance you already know what this piece is about. You may have sat in a waiting room that felt unbearable, or have been told that your struggles are “just part of being Autistic”. You may have found therapy so poorly matched to how your mind works that you left feeling more confused and more alone than when you arrived.

You are not imagining it, the barriers are real, they are well-documented, and they run through the whole system.

This piece is an attempt to name those barriers clearly; not to discourage anyone from seeking help, but because naming them honestly is the first step toward changing them. And because people who are struggling deserve to understand why accessing autism and mental health support is so hard, rather than concluding that they are simply too difficult to help.

Diagnostic Overshadowing: When Everything Gets Blamed On Autism

Diagnostic overshadowing is one of the most significant and least-discussed barriers in autism and mental health care. It happens when a clinician attributes a person’s distress, symptoms, or behavioural changes to their autism diagnosis; rather than recognising them as indicators of a separate, treatable mental or physical health condition.

Anxiety that has become disabling? “That’s part of autism.” Depression so severe a person can barely get out of bed? “Autistic people often struggle with motivation.” Trauma responses from years of masking and chronic stress? “Autistic people can be quite rigid and reactive.”

When every symptom is absorbed into the autism label, mental health needs become invisible, and invisible needs don’t get treated.

Research consistently shows that Autistic people have significantly elevated rates of anxiety, depression, PTSD, OCD, and eating disorders. These are not simply autism traits. They are co-occurring conditions that deserve proper assessment and proper care, overshadowing denies that care before it has even been considered.

Communication Barriers In Standard Talking Therapies

Most mainstream talking therapies, such as CBT, traditional counselling models, and psychodynamic approaches, were developed without Autistic or Neurodivergent people in mind. They are built around assumptions about how people communicate, process emotions, and understand social context that do not hold across all neurotypes.

Standard CBT asks people to identify automatic thoughts, challenge cognitive distortions, and make intuitive links between feelings and behaviours. For someone who processes emotions differently, or who experiences alexithymia, the reduced ability to identify and describe internal emotional states, this model can feel not just unhelpful but actively alienating. Being repeatedly invited to do something you are neurologically wired to find difficult, in a context where struggling is framed as resistance, is not therapy. It is another experience of being told you are doing it wrong.

ADHD can introduce its own specific communication dynamics; variable working memory in sessions, difficulty with the open-ended structure of some therapeutic approaches, time blindness that makes weekly 50-minute appointments feel incoherent. These are not failures of commitment. They are aspects of a neurology that standard therapy formats were never designed to accommodate.

For Autistic people specifically, mental health therapy that does not account for these differences risks causing harm rather than providing relief.

Sensory And Environmental Barriers In Clinical Settings

The mental health system is full of sensory environments that Autistic people have to actively manage just to get through the door. Fluorescent lighting. Rooms that carry the ambient sounds of a busy building, furniture that is uncomfortable in ways that are hard to explain but impossible to ignore, the expectation of sustained eye contact with a relative stranger as a marker of engagement and trust.

When a person is spending significant cognitive and sensory resources on simply tolerating the environment, very little is left for the work of therapy itself. Clinicians who are not trained in the sensory dimensions of autism may read this as disengagement, avoidance, or lack of motivation, when in fact their client is doing an enormous amount of hidden work just to be present.

Studies indicate that Autistic adults are significantly more likely to discontinue talking therapy early than non-Autistic peers, not because they are unwilling to engage, but because the format and environment create barriers that are rarely acknowledged or adapted for. Remote and hybrid therapy options, introduced widely during the pandemic, have been reported by many Autistic people as genuinely more accessible. That finding deserves to permanently shape how autism and mental health services are designed and delivered.

Waiting Lists And The Compounding Of Complex Needs

NHS mental health waiting times are a crisis that affects everyone. But for Autistic and neurodivergent people, who are statistically more likely to present with complex or co-occurring conditions, the consequences of long waits are compounding and severe.

Autistic burnout, the state of deep physical, cognitive, and emotional exhaustion that can follow sustained masking and sensory overload, does not stabilise while someone is on a waiting list. A person who enters a waiting list in crisis may, by the time their appointment arrives months later, be in a significantly worse position than when they were first assessed. The triage criteria that placed them at a particular point on the list may no longer reflect their actual need.

For those waiting for a formal autism or ADHD diagnosis, the picture is bleaker still. Even with a diagnosis, access to many specialist mental health services is closed, if those services were ever available in the first place. Yet, the process of seeking diagnosis, the uncertainty, the self-advocacy required, the exposure to systems that are frequently dismissive, is itself a significant source of distress. People are being harmed by the very process they must navigate to be recognised as needing help.

The connection between autism and mental health is structural. The delays, the gatekeeping, the diagnostic requirements: all of it has a mental health cost.

Join Our Community

This gap is not a personal failing on the part of individual clinicians. It is a systemic failure of training curricula, professional standards, and commissioning priorities. Its consequences are deeply personal; a therapist who does not understand monotropism

posts.title: How We Know Autism
posts.excerpt: An exploration of how we understand autism as Autistic people from session one or Embracing Our Autistic Selves.
posts.text:
Reclaiming the Story of Who We Are

By David Gray-Hammond | NeuroHub Community | Mindfully Divergent Program | May 2026

What is the story you were given about autism; and did it match the life you were actually living? The first module of Embracing Our Autistic Selves opened with that question, and over ninety minutes, a rich, sometimes painful, always illuminating conversation unfolded. This post gathers the key threads.

When I first heard the word autism, it was described to me as a person trapped inside their own little world; living in a bubble, cut off and unreachable. For a long time, I tried to fit that description, but something never quite added up.

“I didn’t feel like I existed in a bubble,” I told the group. “If anything, I felt so connected to the world that it was overwhelming. It was bombarding me at all angles. I didn’t feel isolated from the world. I just didn’t feel like I belonged there; and maybe that was partly because of descriptions like that one.”

That mismatch, between the story handed down and the life actually lived, is exactly what this course, part of NeuroHub’s Mindfully Divergent program, is designed to address. Module 1, How We Know Autism, invites participants to look honestly at where our understanding of autism comes from, whose interests it has served, and what it might mean to step outside it.

— THE FIRST WORD —

When Did You First Hear The Word “Autism”?

The session opened with a deceptively simple question: When did you first hear the word autism, and what did it mean to you in that moment? The answers came from every direction of the group and told a story all by themselves.

FROM THE DISCUSSION

“Because I’m an old person who grew up in the 60s and 70s, I knew it from just the total stereotypical version; an insult. The film Rain Man. The different people, the severe othering. I think that’s why it took me decades to recognise it in myself, because of the stereotype of the male version. I don’t think it even occurred to me that females could have it.” — Participant

“The first time I heard about autism was when someone had brought it to my parents’ attention when I was at school. But they said it would have been noticed by now, as I’m 22, they said if it was autism, I would have been noticed as a child.” — Participant

“My first encounter was watching a programme in the 70s about a young man who could draw the whole of St Pancras Station from memory. The programme was set up as though he was an incredible freak. I remember feeling two things: complete wonder at the detail he could recall; and then fear, because the people watching it with me just projected their own fear. They couldn’t see the wonder.” — Participant

There is something poignant and instructive in this exercise. Nearly every first encounter with the word “autism” was coloured by othering, fear, or the narrowest imaginable picture of what autism could look like; almost always male, almost always white, almost always signified by either savant ability or severe impairment. The message received, almost universally, was: autism is something to fear, avoid, or be relieved you don’t have.

Which means that for the many people who went on to discover they were autistic themselves, that was the identity they had to first confront — and then, painstakingly, undo.

— FEAR OF DIFFERENCE —

The Uncanny Valley And The Fear Of Being Human, Differently

One observation about fear became a thread I pulled on. There is a concept sometimes applied to Autistic experience called the Uncanny Valley effect, the notion that when we perceive something as almost-but-not-quite human, we experience an instinctive revulsion. Some researchers have argued that this is what happens in many people’s responses to Autistic people: we are human, but a different kind of human, and society has been trained to fear difference.

“Difference is not a scary thing, it is a vital part of human existence. It’s something we require as a species in order to exist. It’s diversity that makes a species strong and sustainable. One of the challenges for us as autistic people is helping others understand the necessity of our existence.” — David Gray-Hammond

Several participants reflected on how that fear had been transmitted through cruel language, through the treatment of children at school, through the way being different was understood as a moral failure rather than a natural variation. One person shared how hearing her grandparents speak about people with disabilities in deeply dehumanising terms had left lasting impressions; impressions that shaped what she understood autism to mean long before she came to understand herself.

— A CONTESTED HISTORY —

How Medicine Made Autism And Who Got Left Out

To understand where we are now, we have to go back. The history of how autism has been clinically framed is longer, messier, and more politically loaded than most people realise.

1920s

Grunya Sukhareva: The Description That Was Buried

Before Leo Kanner, before Hans Asperger, a Ukrainian-Jewish psychiatrist named Grunya Sukhareva was writing about children whose experiences we would now recognise as autistic. Crucially, she described them in more affirming terms, not as defective, but as different. Her work was largely erased. She was Jewish, Ukrainian, and, as Helen pointedly added in the session, she was female. Those three facts were more than enough for her insights to be discredited and ignored for decades. Only in recent years has her work begun to resurface.

1940s–1950s

Leo Kanner And “Classic Autism”

Leo Kanner is commonly credited as the first to formally conceptualise autism, what people still call “classic autism” today. His model emphasised delayed language development, difficulties with social communication, fixed and repetitive interests, and repetitive movement. Kanner’s research was conducted almost exclusively on a narrow sample: white, European, male children. The limitations of that sample would go on to shape autism research and diagnosis for decades.

1940s–1970s

Hans Asperger: The Ethical Shadow

Hans Asperger, whose name became synonymous with one presentation of autism, was, as far as the historical record indicates, a Nazi sympathiser whose work involved sorting Autistic children into categories of usefulness to the regime. Those deemed capable were protected, those deemed unproductive were handed over to their deaths. I was direct: “There was an attitude of saving the useful ones whilst disposing of the unuseful ones. And that attitude, you could argue, is still present today; we may approach it differently, but it hasn’t fully gone.”

1950s–1970s

Bruno Bettelheim And The “Refrigerator Mother”

Bettelheim’s theory that autism was caused by cold, emotionally distant parenting, the infamous “refrigerator mother”. This was eventually debunked, but its legacy has proved remarkably durable. The burden of blame fell almost entirely on mothers, a pattern that has never fully disappea

posts.title: Lilipadding, Monotropic Split, and Autistic Burnout
posts.excerpt: A practical guide to understanding why autistic and monotropic people experience burnout, and how the frameworks of monotropic split and lilipadding offer a path toward sustainable living.
posts.text:
For a long time, something was missing from conversations around Autistic wellbeing. Terms like masking, inertia, double empathy, and autistic burnout were beginning to enter the discourse, but a gap remained; a plain, workable explanation for why so many autistic and monotropic people end up in crisis again and again, and what to do about it once they get there.

Tanya Adkin, an autistic ADHD adult, parent of neurodivergent children, and social care professional with a master’s degree in autism, and David Gray Hammond, CEO of NeuroHub Community, a peer mentor of nearly a decade, and both published researchers in autism and substance use, found they were thinking about the same questions from complementary directions. Together, they began naming things that had always existed but lacked language.

Two of those things are monotropic split and lilipadding. Understood together, they offer something rare; not just a description of what goes wrong, but a way of actually moving forward.

Lilipadding And Monotropic Split by David Gray-Hammond
Autistic Storytime With David
Read on Substack

What Does It Mean To Be Monotropic?

Monotropism, first written about in the early 1990s and developed further by autistic researchers, describes a distinct attentional style. Everyone has a finite pool of attentional resources. The difference is in how those resources are deployed. Neurotypical, or polytropic attention, spreads across many things on a more superficial level, like a flashlight illuminating a wide area at relatively low intensity. Monotropic attention works differently; it concentrates deeply on fewer things at once, going narrow and intense rather than broad and shallow.

A useful analogy from David’s and Helen Edgar’s Re-Storying Autism course; it is the difference between snorkelling and scuba diving, both people are in the water, but a snorkeller sits at the surface, dipping in and out freely. A scuba diver goes deep, and cannot shoot back to the surface without consequences. Come up too fast, and you get the bends.

This is not a deficit. It is a different architecture of attention, one that produces the sustained depth of focus enabling genuine expertise, intense creative flow, and profound connection. However, it creates a specific vulnerability; when the world demands that you constantly shift attention, split it, redirect it, or manage multiple competing streams at once, the cost is enormous.

Monotropic Split: The Vehicle That Carries Autistic People Into Crisis

The concept Tanya developed is disarmingly simple, which is part of why it resonates so widely. Monotropic split is what happens when a monotropic person is forced to divide their attention in ways that do not match how their attentional system naturally works, and the competing demands are so persistent that they have no choice but to try to give more attention than they have.

Tanya describes the moment she realised she had named something new; she was in a virtual meeting and mentioned casually, assuming it was common knowledge, “the monotropic split thing, you know, where we’re forced to constantly divide our attention, and it causes burnout, and meltdown, and shutdown, and crisis”. She had, without realising it, conceptualised something that existed but had no name.

David describes what monotropic split feels like from the inside:

“Imagine my attention as a sheet of fabric with nerve endings, so I can feel what it’s doing. Monotropic split feels like that fabric being torn. It’s like a cognitive injury. It cognitively hurts.”

The outside picture is harder to pin down, and this is why Tanya and David are both critical of checklist-based models; there is no single presentation. Monotropic split can manifest as autistic burnout, the most frequently discussed expression, it can look like what Tanya calls meerkat mode; a state of hypervigilance and heightened anxiety. For David, who experiences psychosis as a co-occurring condition, sustained monotropic split has carried him toward paranoia and psychotic breakdown. It can feel like emotional numbness, paralysis, or choice overwhelm; the sense of failing at something everyone else seems to manage effortlessly.

What this looks like externally varies for every person. What is shared is the underlying mechanism, too many demands, pulling too hard, on a system built for depth rather than breadth.

What Creates Monotropic Split?

Almost anything that demands attentional resources simultaneously. An Autistic child in a mainstream classroom navigating 30 other children, a changing cast of adults, sensory inputs across every channel, social expectations, masking demands, and an academic curriculum, all at once, for six hours a day. An Autistic parent with a newborn who is never off duty, never able to close an attentional channel. A professional managing Slack, emails, in-person meetings, and continuous social demands in real time.

Importantly, the source of split does not need to be directly aimed at you. David points out something often overlooked; if your close friend is in conflict with someone else, not involving you at all, this can still affect you, because it changes your relationship with your friend. The emotional states of people we are close to create ripple effects through our attentional system, even when we have no direct stake in what is happening.

Thinking about monotropic split ecologically, as something shaped by a whole system of environments, from your own body outward to institutional and political forces, matters enormously here. The distress is real, but its origin is rarely personal failure. As David puts it; what often feels like a personal failing, such as Autistic burnout, is really an inevitability produced by a vast ecosystem not built for the way we process the world.

Autistic Mental Health Conference 2026

Lilipadding: A Framework For Transitions And Recovery From Autistic Burnout

If monotropic split explains the mechanism of crisis, lilipadding is the answer to what you do about it, both during autistic burnout and in the daily work of preventing it. The metaphor comes from the image of crossing a pond by moving from one lily pad to the next, rather than attempting a single impossible leap to the far bank.

In its simplest form, lilipadding is a way of honouring monotropic transitions. As monotropic people, transitions are genuinely costly, pulling attention from one thing and placing it somewhere new is not the quick manoeuvre it might be for someone with polytropic attention. When neurotypical environments expect instant transitions, a lunch bell rings, a meeting ends, a task switches, the mismatch between what is expected and what our attentional system can readily do produces distress, often misread as stubbornness or dysregulation.

Lilipadding works with that reality rather than against it. Instead of expecting a single, immediate transition, you introduce intermediary step, lily pads, that follow the natural associat

A growing movement of Autistic-led education and community-building is rewriting the narrative. And at the our part of that movement is NeuroHub Community ; a neuro-affirming space founded by Autistic people, for anyone who wants to understand neurodivergent lives more deeply

Who it’s for: Autistic adults who want to reconnect with themselves, build self-acceptance, and find community along the way.

Who it’s for: Professionals working with Autistic people, parents, educators, and anyone in a position to change how autism is understood in their community.
