A behind-the-scenes look into the collaborative workflow between Helen Edgar ( Autistic Realms ) and Ryan Boren ( Stimpunks ) as we write about Neuroqueer Learning Spaces (NQLS) and continue our neuroqueering journeys, connecting with awe-inspiring people and discovering new ideas to explore along the way.

Liminal Spaces

Ryan Boren ( Stimpunks ) and I are neuroqueering ourselves and the spaces we work in as we write about NQLS. We met online in 2022 in the liminal spaces between various online neurodivergent communities, both constantly feeling on the edge of things, even in the most neuro-inclusive settings and groups we could find.

We are both autistic and multiply neurodivergent and deeply passionate about working towards radical inclusivity. Due to our lived experience as parents and professionals, we have seen first-hand the harm that the heavy burden of cisheteronormativity, neuronormativity and neuro-essentialism is causing, especially to neurodivergent people. Normativity is breaking people’s mental and physical health and severely destroying the tremendous potential that is inside everyone. We need to find caring spaces to connect with others, to create an ecological system of care (Bettin, AutCollab ), a responsive space that enables authenticity and values the potential of everyone, regardless of neurology, disability, race, gender or any other intersection that is marginalised.

Liminality

by Carrie Newcomer (2021)

So much of what we know
Lives just below the surface.
Half of a tree
Spreads out beneath our feet.
Living simultaneously in two worlds,
Each half informing and nurturing
The whole.
A tree is either and neither
But mostly both.

I am drawn to liminal spaces,
The half-tamed and unruly patch
Where the forest gives way
And my little garden begins.
Where water, air and light overlap
Becoming mist on the morning pond.

I like to sit on my porch steps, barn jacket and boots
In the last long exhale of the day,
When bats and birds loop in and then out,
One rising to work,
One readying for sleep.

And although the full moon calls the currents,
And the dark moon reminds me that my best language
Has always emerged out of the silence ,
It is in the waxing and waning
Where I most often live,
Neither here nor there,
But simply On the way.

There are endings and beginnings
One emerging out of the other.
But most days I travel in an ever present
And curious now.
A betwixt and between,
That is almost,
But not quite,
The beautiful,
But not yet.

I’ve been learning to live with what is,
More patient with the process,
To love what is becoming ,
And the questions that keep returning.

I am learning to trust
The horizon I walk toward
Is an orientation
Not a destination
And that I will keep catching glimpses
Of something great and luminous
From the corner of my eye.

I am learning to live where losses hold fast
And grief lets loose and unravels.
Where a new kind of knowing can pick up the thread.

Where I can slide palms with a paradox
And nod at the dawn,
As the shadows pull back
And spirit meets bone.

Carrie Newcomer (2021)
From Until Now: New Poems by Carrie Newcomer. Copyright © 2021 Carrie Newcomer. Published by Available Light Publishing

Our Neuroqueer Learning Spaces project is born largely from trauma, grief and a shared passion for challenging, deconstructing and re-imagining what our education and healthcare system could be like if people were prepared to unlearn and unleash their bodyminds from the weight of conforming to neuronormative, socially constructed ways of being. The pressure to ‘fit in’ is real and intense, and neuronormativity is limiting for everyone (not just neurodivergent people).

The pressures and barriers to education and health care we have endured and are still battling against are heavy. It has left us, like so many other people in our situation,feeling broken and ‘weathered like sea glass’ (Shepherd et al.,2024) . As part of NQLS, we have created a community-driven NQLS Manifesto and an NQLS Open Framework of Guidance . We are also in the process of developing anti-behaviourism resources to help parents/carers and professionals and those they support to challenge harmful practices, such as (Applied Behaviour Analysis) ABA and (Positive Behaviour Support) PBS. These WHY SHEET resources are free open license and can be edited and used to help self advocate for young people who may be facing barriers accessing education.

If you value this project, please consider signing our WHY Sheet endorsement page along with many other parents/carers and professionals to help give confidence, agency and autonomy to those needing these resources.

Inspired by the quote from Audre Lorde (1984), “The master’s tools will never dismantle the master’s hous e”, we are advocating a need to:

“Queer the system, queer the tools and create new tools.”

(Nick Walker, 2024)

Our Neuroqueering Journeys

Trust

Where my voice has often felt dismissed as a parent, it is often validated, listened to and sought as a professional. Trust is an issue. Different voices are trusted by different people, in different places. Safe spaces are needed to develop trust, and time is needed to be with people to gain trust. Reaching out and connecting takes courage; there is always a doubt as to whether you are really in a safe space where you can truly trust and be trusted. There is a vulnerability in admitting things aren’t working, exploring what is under the surface, finding people to connect with who share your struggles and ethos, and having a shared hope for change to find a way out of difficult situations. We need spaces where we feel safe and where there is trust so that we can unlearn and relearn and continue to neuroqueer.

As a white professional person, being a part of both the neurodivergent parent/carer communities and the professional education and healthcare communities, I am aware I am in a unique and relatively safe position of privilege to even write and explore this topic. Enforced hierarchy and the double empathy problem (Milton, 2012) are at the root of so many difficulties and often result in the voices of neurodivergent or disabled people being dismissed. At best, voices may be silenced, and at worse, lived experience can be so deeply misunderstood and misinterpreted it can lead to accusations of not parenting ‘right’, being sent on courses to try and make families conform to neuronoramtive ideals, or in some of the most severe cases we have seen lead to accusations of neglect, FII and safeguarding concerns ( Shona Murphy ).

Trust, safe spaces, and community are vital to NQLS and our own personal neuroqueering journeys. When the world feels unsafe, you need to create your own spaces and make your own connections. We think creating neuroqueer learning spaces is one possibility that is worth exploring.

Can We Trust?

by Pernille Fraser (2019)

Can we trust the space you offer?
Can we trust the words you utter?

Can we trust the time decided?
Can we tr

posts.text:
Neuroqueer Learning Spaces Webinar — A summary and reflection

Neuroqueer Learning Spaces is a community project led by Ryan Boren ( Stimpunks ) and Helen Edgar ( Autistic Realms ).
More information is available on Stimpunks’ website.

To support this project and open up further discussions about neuroqueering education and learning spaces, David Gray-Hammond hosted a live webinar, “ Explore Neuroqueer Learning Spaces,” with Dr. Nick Walker on 6 May 2024. This is available to watch via David’s Emergent Divergence website and on Facebook & YouTube .

All quotes are taken directly from this webinar unless otherwise stated.

What is neuroqueering?

Nick began the webinar by reminding us that ‘Neuroqueer theory is an extension of queer theory into the realm of neurodiversity”. Everyone can neuroqueer. Neuroqueering is not limited to people who are innately neurodivergent and also queer; neuroqueering is open for everyone to explore.

Neurodivergent people can neuroqueer and diverge themselves into ever-expanding neuroqueer ways of being. Neurotypical people can engage in neuroqueering to diverge their bodyminds further and liberate themselves from socially instilled norms.

Neuroqueering is an act; it has intent; we can neuroqueer how we live and how we experience, interact, engage and respond to the world around us. Within our neuroqueer learning spaces, we are exploring how neurotypicality, which is socially constructed, can be queered to liberate bodyminds. As part of our Stimpunks Learning Spaces project, Ryan and I are also exploring the benefits and potential of embracing an embodied education within our neuroqueer learning spaces. An embodied education is also something that Nick expanded upon and stressed the importance of as she shared some examples of her practice within this webinar.

“Neuroqueer theory is about creative neurodivergence” (Nick Walker)

What if…?

“Neurotypicality is limiting” (Walker). Neuroqueering involves engaging with life and opening up possibilities. Neuroqueering expands potential, questions boundaries and subverts normality. It enables us to explore, to try, to be curious; it opens up questions and the potential of ‘ What if…? ’

The potential of ‘What if?’ is often found in children’s excitement, awe and wonder as they playfully explore the world around them. They may excitedly run up to you with a twig or shiny stone they have found, wanting to share that moment of finding something that fills them with joy and curisoity and is reflective of the pure magic of being alive and discovering the wonder of the world. Over time, the awe of finding the ‘Marvellous in the Real’ (Grand, 1978) often becomes eroded in people due to the neuronormative expectations that weigh down on our bodyminds to behave, act, talk and even only show joy in certain ways.

Nick and David expanded on this by referring to Nick’s writing about hand movements and stimming, which is also explored in Neuroqueer Heresies (2021, p183–191). There are often enforced school rules based on neuronormative values and expectations for having “quiet hands”, doing “good sitting”, doing “good looking” (making eye contact with the teacher in class) and demonstrating attention skills in specific ways. The use of Positive Behaviour Support(PBS) plans and Applied Behaviour Analysis (ABA) to reinforce certain behaviours and actions, such as ‘quiet hands’ has been proven to cause considerable harm and trauma, especially for autistic people as it aims to suppress and eradicate their innate need to regulate by stimming and expressing themselves authentically. There is a comprehensive resource list about the harm of behaviourism on Stimpunks website. We are also creating “ Why ” sheets to help parents and professionals advocate and provide neurodiversity affirming alternatives to support young people.

Many other questions were posed throughout the webinar, including:

How do we queer neuronormativity?

How do we queer our bodyminds?

What does this look like in a learning space?

(We hope to expand these webinars so we can loop back to some of these questions and the comments raised in the text chat. )

Systems

Nick and David briefly (it is a huge topic!) talked about systemic oppression and agreed that education needs a system of some kind. We can not just destroy the education system; it is not practical or realistic. Some parts can be used or at least transformed. We can neuroqueer the education system.

People need structure; routines are as important in neuroqueer learning spaces as they are everywhere else. Routines provide feelings of safety and reduce anxiety. More flexibility is needed for people to be responsive and open to change and transformation. We need to ask what our routines look like, what purpose they have, and what use are they? How responsive and adaptable are they? Are they created in collaboration with others?

Inspired by the quote from Audre Lorde (1984), “ The master’s tools will never dismantle the master’s house ”, Nick said that we don’t need to burn the system down; instead, we should:

“Queer the system, queer the tools and create new tools.” (Nick Walker)

David highlighted that contemporary approaches to research looking at the oppressive structures of our education system are often reactionary, suggesting systems are torn down; however, this could be a barrier in itself to neuroqueering. If you are focused on tearing down the system, you are not neuroqueering. Neuroqueering is not destructive; it is transformative.

To neuroqueer is to transform, not destroy. (Helen Edgar)

Based on the work of Stafford Beer ’s cybernetic principles, Nick suggests that it is not necessarily the idea of systems and hierarchy that are the problem; instead, it is the way neuronormative ideals currently enforce them. We need more flexibility and collaborative, interdisciplinary approaches.

To what extent are some parts of the current system repurposable?

Can we remake the tools, and create new tools?

What do we want to dismantle, and what do we want to reshape?

Space

How can we queer our physical learning spaces to free the body?

Nick shared her experiences as a professor, and she emphasised the importance of being a facilitator of learning. She shared with us how she values adopting a collaborative approach to learning where students are not passive recipients but are co-creators. She asks her students to question what knowledge they bring to their learning space so everyone can learn together.

Nick provides a liberating neuroqueer space for students to express their ways of sharing the knowledge they have gained and collaborating with others. Not enforcing neurotypical ways of demonstrating t ways (tests or enables people to express themselves in ways that suit them, whether through art, poetry or other forms of self-expression. This way of working leans nicely into the courses Nick delivers and facilitates. It would be interesting to know what neuroqueer learning

I also live much of my life in and between the online (primarily neurodivergent) […]
posts.text:
I am starting my new blog in the middle. I am in the middle of what is known as ‘midlife’ as I am forty-five; I am also mid-career, having resigned from teaching and not yet working in any other defined role. I also live much of my life in and between the online (primarily neurodivergent) communities.

These spaces have become my places of safety, support, and escapism and are a wonderful opportunity to develop connections. Henri Lefebvre (1991), in his work The Production of Space , explores the concept of space being a ‘living space’. Lefebvre wrote, “ Nothing disappears completely… In space, what came earlier continues to underpin what follows… Pre-existing space underpins not only durable spatial arrangements but also representational spaces and their attendant imagery and mythic narratives .”

Lefebvre’s ideas support my thoughts around the concept of space being alive; I feel space (like our own identity and energy) is fluid. Space constantly changes and depends on the interactions of those around us and objects within other spaces. I am exploring ways of finding meaning in the spaces within what could be considered ‘ma’ to enable thoughts to develop and create connections with others. I believe this could be seen as a form of neuroqueering as defined in Nick Walker’s (2021) book Neuroqueer Heresie s. I am considering if the energy created by these connections can lead to even more new spaces, ideas, and possibilities by subverting the expectations of the normativity of relationships and communication.

‘Ma’ is a Japanese concept and has no English equivalent but can be loosely translated as the space between things or a pause between events. Fletcher (2001), in The Art of Looking Sideways, quotes Isaac Stern as describing music as “that little bit between each note — silences which give the form”. In their book A Thousand Plateaus , Deleuze and Guattari (1980) explore the concept of a ‘rhizomatic’ model of thought and ‘shifting bodies’. I have been thinking about how ‘ma’ relates Deleuze and Guattari’s philosophy and neuroqueering by enabling the physical space between people to create the potential for energy to grow.

In our everyday lives, at this very moment, people are joining online communities for information, to seek understanding, and connecting with others. The general themes of this blog series will include an exploration of; the philosophy of Deleuze, the history of art (specifically the minimalist movement), the connections between language and the forming of relationships and an exploration of Nick Walker’s (2021) theory of neuroqueering . I aim to demonstrate how we can find a space to nourish and support mental well-being at some intersection between these concepts and topics for those interested and open to exploring these ideas.

I can already feel a deep flow weaving between these topics, even though that is currently happening in a slow, fuzzy, hazy way. My own thoughts will inevitably be shaped by the interactions and discussions I have with others about these subjects. I aim to create a singular, more coherent chapter which will contribute towards a larger anthology of work from within the community interested in neuroqueer theory. I want to be transparent about my aim with anyone who engages in shared stories and conversations with me on this journey. I value connections and collaboration and hope this will draw various people and communities together that are interested and resonate with some of these ideas.

In 1943, T.S. Eliot’s collection of four poems were collated to form Four Quartets . The final poem in this series Little Gidding (1942), continues Eliot’s exploration of time and our connections with each other through generations and current society.

“ What we call the beginning is often the end. And to make an end is to make a beginning. The end is where we start from.”

This quote seems particularly relevant to my deep interest in evolving spirals and finding meaning in gaps and spaces. I am returning to themes I started exploring almost 25–30 years ago from the new perspective and understanding of my autistic identity and, more recently, through an exploration of neuroqueering.

I visualise relationships and ways of being as constantly evolving spirals that spin in and out in a multidimensional way. Different connections and experiences add to and contribute to a wider, deeper fluid rhizomatic network of potential that is always in a constant state of flux. This idea of an evolving spiral and returning to a new beginning in the middle is beautifully reflected in Eliot’s poem Little Gidding :

“ We shall not cease from exploration
And the end of all our exploring
Will be to arrive where we started
And know the place for the first time.
Through the unknown, remembered gate
When the last of earth left to discover
Is that which was the beginning;
At the source of the longest river
The voice of the hidden waterfall
And the children in the apple-tree
Not known, because not looked for
But heard, half-heard, in the stillness
Between two waves of the sea” .

— T.S. Eliot, from “Little Gidding,” Four Quartets (Gardners Books; Main edition, April 30, 2001) Originally published 1943.”

I have struggled to start this blog as I believe there is no definitive way to start anything; finding a specific point of anything is impossible as there will always be multiple folds, pleats and deeper intersections, which could be classed as a ‘start’. I see this as trying to find a space ‘ between two waves of the sea ’ as Eliot wrote. There will always be something preceding and will always be another connection and intersection. However, if we can open our bodyminds, we can find moments of stillness, a pause, and meaning can grow from within the spaces between objects and others; this is where creativity and potential evolves.

In The Fold (1988), Deleuze explores this idea in his first chapter, ‘ The Pleats of Matter ’ by drawing on the work of Leibniz and Monadology (1714) in a beautiful description which summarises the infinite amount of folds and pleats that can occur within origami where, the ‘ a fold is always folded within a fold, like a cavern in a cavern ’. This concept of the monad further explores the folds of time and space as a continuous process of ‘becoming.’ This is something I will be returning to.

Throughout my following few blogs, I aim to ‘unfold’ and explore The Fold and other writing more deeply. I see these folds as a fluid state rather than a defined line, and it is within this fluidity that neuroqueering ideas can be further explored too. I visualise this being similar to the autistic experience of monotropism . This concept evolved from the work of Murray, Lawson and Lesser (2005), which I will also return to in a future blog; I see this as a way of identifying and understanding my experiences and how I relate to others.

Deleuze’s idea of folds and pleats fits into my interpretation of neuroqueering, which allows infinite p

posts.text:
Statement of Purpose

• Helen Edgar – More Realms (the Organisation , we , our or us ) is committed to preventing and responding to risks of harm to and promoting the welfare of all children and adults at risk that we work with (i.e. as Helen Edgar – More Realms’s clients). These individuals are referred to as the ‘ Beneficiaries ’ of this Safeguarding Policy.

• We recognise the importance of this commitment to safety and welfare and, further, are committed to safeguarding all Beneficiaries without discrimination due to an individual’s age, disability, race, religion or belief, sex, gender reassignment, pregnancy or maternity leave status, marriage or civil partnership status, or sexual orientation.

• This Safeguarding Policy is based on the safeguarding laws of England, Wales, and Scotland, including related guidance issued by the UK Government and relevant governmental departments, agencies, and public bodies. If this Policy is at any time inconsistent with this body of law, Helen Edgar – More Realms will act to meet the requirements of up-to-date safeguarding laws in priority to the requirements set out in this Policy.

• Helen Edgar – More Realms has implemented this Safeguarding Policy in order to meet its obligations as an organisation working with children and adults at risk.

• Any questions in relation to this Policy should be referred to Helen Edgar Founder in the first instance, by emailing autisticrealms@gmail.com.

Scope of this Safeguarding Policy

• This Policy explains key aspects of how Helen Edgar – More Realms prevents harm in relation to its Beneficiaries via its practices and its Staff Members’ conduct.

• This Safeguarding Policy covers the organisation and operation of all of Helen Edgar – More Realms’s activities involving children and adults at risk (i.e. our Relevant Activities ). These primarily include:

• Providing Education and Training Resources.

• Providing Workshops to offer support and guidance to families.

• Education Consultant/Advisor Family Support Worker.

• Coaching/Mentoring.

• Author/Writer

• This Policy’s guidelines and obligations apply to all individuals working for or acting on behalf of Helen Edgar – More Realms in the UK at all levels, including senior managers, officers, employees, consultants, trainees, homeworkers, part-time and fixed-term workers, casual workers, agency workers, volunteers, and interns (collectively ‘ Staff Members ’).

• This Policy does not form part of any contract of employment or similar and Helen Edgar – More Realms may amend it at any time at our absolute discretion.

Defining Safeguarding

• ‘Safeguarding’ is an umbrella term that refers to work (e.g. practices and procedures) aimed at preventing or responding to harm or risks of harm posed to vulnerable individuals, and at promoting these individuals’ wider welfare. Safeguarding is particularly important for children and adults at risk. Most safeguarding legal obligations relate to the care of these groups and these are the groups to whom the protections set out in this Policy apply. For safeguarding purposes:

• Children are individuals younger than 18 years old.

• Adults at risk are individuals 18 years old or over (in England and Wales) or 16 years old or over (in Scotland) who have care and/or support needs and who are, because of these needs, unable to protect themselves from harm (e.g. due to illness or disability). This need not be on a permanent basis.

• The commitments and practices contained in this Safeguarding Policy apply to the safeguarding of Helen Edgar – More Realms’s Beneficiaries from harm caused by either:

• The activities and practices of Helen Edgar – More Realms and any conduct of its Staff Members, or

• People and situations outside of Helen Edgar – More Realms and its Staff Members’ control, where Helen Edgar – More Realms’s Staff Members are aware of, ought to be aware of, or reasonably suspect the risks posed by a situation.

• For the purposes of this Policy, a ‘ Safeguarding Concern ’ is any conduct or situation that is known or reasonably suspected by a Staff Member or another party that risks violating the safeguarding commitments set out above.

Key Measures that Helen Edgar – More Realms is Committed to Implementing and Maintaining to Safeguard its Beneficiaries

• Ensuring that Staff Members are trained to, and encouraged to, report any Safeguarding Concerns that they identify. Staff Members will be encouraged to follow Helen Edgar – More Realms’s safeguarding reporting procedures as closely as possible when reporting concerns (set out below under the heading ‘ Procedures: Reporting ’).

• Ensuring that all Staff Members listen to all safeguarding-related queries and concerns raised by other Staff Members, Beneficiaries, or relevant other parties, with respect and professionalism. Staff Members should be trained how to, and encouraged to, then assist with reporting any such concerns via Helen Edgar – More Realms’s regular reporting procedures.

• Procedures will be designed to ensure all safeguarding issues are dealt with fairly and objectively even when allegations are made against one of Helen Edgar – More Realms’s Staff Members. Any such allegations will be treated in a manner that takes into account the gravity of the accusations, but which does not vilify or presume the guilt of an accused individual without a fair investigation.

• Any reports that qualify as protected disclosures under whistleblowing law will be treated securely and in a protected manner in line with whistleblowing law.

posts.title: penguin pebbling
posts.excerpt: Penguin Pebbling: a neuro-affirming card game of belonging and connection by Helen Edgar and Ryan Boren, now at penguinpebbling.app.
posts.text:
A collaboration between Helen Edgar of Autistic Realms and Ryan Boren, Stimpunks Foundation

Penguin Pebbling is a card game about belonging. There are no winners, no scores and no pressure to perform. You draw a card, share in whatever way feels right, and pass a real pebble to someone when what they have shared lands with you. You can leave whenever you need to, and you can always pass.

Ryan and I made the game together, and it now has a home of its own at penguinpebbling.app (Edgar & Boren, 2026). You can play it right there in your browser, drawing cards one at a time and filtering them by love locution, or print the full deck to hold in your hands. There are Plain Language and Easy Read guides too, so everyone can join in.

Did you know?

Some penguins, such as gentoos, build their nests from pebbles and offer pebbles to one another. I first wrote about penguin pebbling as an Autistic love language in 2023: the small gifts we pass to people we care about, like a stick or a stone, a link, a song, a picture or an interesting fact, which quietly say “I saw this and thought of you” (Edgar, 2023). It is one of the Five Neurodivergent Love Locutions coined by Amythest Schaber (Neurowonderful), alongside infodumping, parallel play, support swapping and deep pressure, which Stimpunks has documented and shared (Stimpunks Foundation, 2022).

The game is grounded in Damian Milton’s double empathy problem, which reminds us that misunderstandings between Autistic and non-Autistic people run in both directions (Milton, 2012), and in monotropism, the theory of how Autistic attention gathers deeply around a few interests at a time (Murray et al., 2005). The love locutions give us a shared language for the ways we already show care, so that our ways of connecting are recognised on their own terms.

How to play

All you need is the cards and a handful of smooth pebbles or other small objects. Everyone begins by holding three pebbles and noticing their weight and texture, and the rest go in the middle as a shared pebble bank.

• 🃏 Draw a card : read it aloud, or ask someone else to read it for you.

• 💬 Share your way : speak, write, draw, use AAC, sign or gesture, whatever feels right. You can always pass, with no explanation needed.

• 🪨 Pass a pebble : when someone’s sharing lands with you, when you feel heard or recognise something, pass them a pebble. If you have none left, take one from the bank, so no one is ever without a way to show they care.

• 🐧 Finish together : set your pebbles down, or agree on a group signal before you begin. The game ends when everyone feels complete for now.

The game is free to use, share and adapt for non-commercial purposes under a CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licence. If you are using it in a clinic, classroom, support group or training, you can support our community-led work by buying the printable card deck from the Autistic Realms shop, and there is a guide for practitioners to go with it.

Play Penguin Pebbling

References

Edgar, H. (2023). Penguin pebbling: An Autistic love language. Autistic Realms . https://autisticrealms.com/penguin-pebbling-an-autistic-love-language/

Edgar, H., & Boren, R. (2026). Penguin Pebbling: A game of creating belonging, building connection and understanding Autistic identity . Autistic Realms & Stimpunks Foundation. https://penguinpebbling.app/

Milton, D. E. M. (2012). On the ontological status of autism: The ‘double empathy problem’. Disability & Society, 27 (6), 883–887. https://doi.org/10.1080/09687599.2012.710008

Murray, D., Lesser, M., & Lawson, W. (2005). Attention, monotropism and the diagnostic criteria for autism. Autism, 9 (2), 139–156. https://doi.org/10.1177/1362361305051398

Stimpunks Foundation. (2022). The five neurodivergent love locutions . https://stimpunks.org/2022/01/22/the-five-neurodivergent-love-languages-2/

posts.title: monotropic map
posts.excerpt: Twenty places a monotropic person goes: Helen Edgar’s Map of Monotropic Experiences, now at monotropicmap.org.
posts.text:
A collaboration between Helen Edgar of Autistic Realms and the Stimpunks Foundation : Ryan Boren, Norah Hobbs and Chelsea Adams

I first drew the Map of Monotropic Experiences in 2024, as a way of showing the places my own Autistic and ADHD bodymind moves through. It became an illustrated island in a blue sea, with twenty named places on and around it, from the Attention Tunnels and the River of Monotropic Flow States to Infodump Canyon, the Lake of Limerence and the Tides of the Sensory Sea. I made it as a map of me, and I have been deeply moved by how many people have told me they found themselves on it too.

Monotropicmap.org is the map’s new home, built together with Ryan, Norah and Chelsea at Stimpunks. Each of the twenty areas now has a page of its own, and every numbered marker on the map opens that area. You can also wander the areas by the kind of place they are: places of flow, places of connection, stuck states and places of pressure. It is a map to find yourself on, so there are no scores, types or results, and no accounts, analytics or tracking either.

Did you know?

Monotropism is a neurodiversity-affirming theory of autism developed by Autistic people, first by Dinah Murray and Wenn Lawson with Mike Lesser (Murray et al., 2005). It describes minds that pull attention strongly towards a small number of interests at any one time, leaving fewer resources for everything else. Things outside the attention tunnel can be missed, and moving between tunnels takes real energy. Autistic, ADHD and AuDHD people are more likely to be monotropic (Garau et al., 2023), and the home of the theory is monotropism.org , looked after by Fergus Murray.

Almost every area on the map was named by somebody, and the site credits each of them and links to their own words. Erin Human gave us tendril theory, Fergus Murray gave us attention tunnels and flow, and Damian Milton gave us the double empathy problem (Milton, 2012). Tanya Adkin and David Gray-Hammond named meerkat mode, Dora Raymaker and colleagues defined Autistic burnout (Raymaker et al., 2020), and Wenn Lawson wrote about object permanence. Penguin pebbling, monotropic time and the Autistic rhizome are mine, and Cavendish Space is Ryan’s.

The water it all sits in

It would be easy to read the map as a portrait of one person and their struggles. Some of its roughest waters, though, such as the Burnout Whirlpools and the Shark Infested Waters of Neuronormativity and Behaviourism, are made by schools, workplaces and clinics built around the idea that there is one correct way to have a mind. So the site also holds a second map, the frame, which looks at who makes that weather in the first place.

Where would you like to go today?

There is no right place to start. You might land in a rabbit hole of research this morning and wash up on the Beach of Body Doubling by the afternoon, and every part of the island is there when you need it.

• 🏝️ The twenty areas : every place on the island, each with its own page, its originator credited and links to further reading.

• 🌊 The frame : the second map, about neuronormative domination and who makes the weather.

• 🎓 Free training : open-source training of about forty-five minutes, for schools, workplaces, health settings and community groups.

• ✏️ Your map : mark the places you find yourself on your own map and share it with the community story project, or draw a new map of your own.

• 🐧 Places that grew their own sites : the Penguin Pebbling Cove became the Penguin Pebbling card game Ryan and I made, the Campsite became the Cavendish Cards , and the Rhizomatic Communities and the Forest of Joy, Awe and Wonder live on at Star Stuff .

The map and everything built from it are shared under a CC BY-SA 4.0 licence, so you are welcome to share it and adapt it, as long as you keep the credit and the licence with it. If you would like to explore your own attention style further, the site links to the Monotropism Questionnaire by Garau et al. (2023).

Explore the Map of Monotropic Experiences

References

Garau, V., Murray, A. L., Woods, R., Chown, N., Hallett, S., Murray, F., Wood, R., & Fletcher-Watson, S. (2023). Development and validation of a novel self-report measure of monotropism in autistic and non-autistic people: The Monotropism Questionnaire [Preprint]. OSF. https://osf.io/ft73y/

Milton, D. E. M. (2012). On the ontological status of autism: The ‘double empathy problem’. Disability & Society, 27 (6), 883–887. https://doi.org/10.1080/09687599.2012.710008

Murray, D., Lesser, M., & Lawson, W. (2005). Attention, monotropism and the diagnostic criteria for autism. Autism, 9 (2), 139–156. https://doi.org/10.1177/1362361305051398

Raymaker, D. M., Teo, A. R., Steckler, N. A., Lentz, B., Scharer, M., Delos Santos, A., Kapp, S. K., Hunter, M., Joyce, A., & Nicolaidis, C. (2020). “Having all of your internal resources exhausted beyond measure and being left with no clean-up crew”: Defining autistic burnout. Autism in Adulthood, 2 (2), 132–143. https://doi.org/10.1089/aut.2019.0079

posts.title: stimpunks world
posts.excerpt: A street where no two rooms are alike: Stimpunks.World, from Stimpunks Foundation.
posts.text:
A Stimpunks Foundation street, with rooms dreamed up by Ryan Boren, Helen Edgar of Autistic Realms and More Realms, and the wider Stimpunks community

Queer without fear. Interdependent and here. Divergent and proud. Living out loud. Those four lines hang over the entrance to Stimpunks.World, and they set the tone for everything you will find once you step onto the street.

Stimpunks.World is a street you can wander at your own pace. Each shopfront opens onto a room with its own colours, its own typefaces and its own mood, and the rooms have been made so that no two of them match. There is a dancefloor and a punk club, a zine table and a comedy club reached down a ramp, a burrow of belonging for burnouts, a samefood café, a relaxed picture house where the house lights stay up, and a Dopamine Dress-Up Den that began as one of my own ideas. Past the treeline there are campgrounds for anyone who would rather not live on a street at all, and past the last streetlight the Outskirts keep their after-dark premises.

At the entrance, a dial asks how loud you would like it, anywhere from Gentle to Max Glitter. The street starts wherever your own device says, and nothing moves, flashes or plays until you choose. That small dial carries a great deal of what we believe about access. Sensory autonomy belongs to the person arriving, and a place can be full of glitter and delight while still letting each of us decide how much of it we take in.

Did you know?

The street has a name, and it belongs to someone else. Danny the Street is a character from DC Comics’ Doom Patrol , created by Grant Morrison and Richard Case in 1990: a living, joyfully gender-nonconforming street who turns up wherever somebody needs shelter and rearranges themselves to suit whoever has arrived (Morrison & Case, 1990). Rooms that refuse to match, a field for those who need to be a little apart, and a shopfront with the keys left in the door all come from Danny, and the site says so proudly.

Most of what Stimpunks makes is careful on purpose, with careful palettes, careful sourcing and careful hedging. Stimpunks.World is the playful other half of that same breath. It keeps just two careful habits. The first is attribution, because crediting people is both a licence and a form of respect, so every song, typeface, quotation and borrowed name is credited in the liner notes. The second is contrast, because clashing colours still need to be readable for everyone who visits (Stimpunks Foundation, 2026).

Where would you like to wander today?

There is no right way round the street, and nothing on it is scored, counted or ranked. You might want the dancefloor on a bright day and the quiet of the burrow by evening, and both are waiting for you.

• 🪩 The rooms : from the Pink Pony Club dancefloor to the Latibulum, the Healing Checkpoint and the Lightbulb Picture House, every shopfront is a small world of its own.

• 🗺️ The Map : the whole street as a white card model on a cutting mat, so you can see where everything stands before you set off.

• 🌿 The Garden : through the gate in the wall, with one bed for every site Stimpunks publishes and the hands that tend each one.

• 🏕️ The Campgrounds : pitches in a field past the treeline, for those who would rather be at peace in nature with the street still in reach.

• 🔑 Your Room : an empty storefront with the keys in the door, waiting for someone in the community to make it their own.

Everything on the street is free to visit, and the street itself rearranges for whoever walks down it. Come as you are, turn the dial to wherever feels right, and wander.

Wander down Stimpunks.World

Come and visit my Faery Yurt

If you follow the fairy lights from the treeline, past the edge of the street and into the campgrounds, you will find my yurt, pitched at the edge of the woods with a stream tracing the trees. It is always night in there, the good kind of night, with candles along the shelves and fairy lights strung low across the canvas so the whole room glows amber. The sofas are far too soft (you sink, and then you stay), the ivy came in through the window frame years ago and was never asked to leave, and the flap of the door is always open. Take your shoes off and stay as long as you need to.

Inside, there is a soundtrack called Faery Yurt’s Yarn , a playlist of the songs I keep coming back to, from Pink Floyd, Kate Bush and AURORA to Portishead, Tracy Chapman, Ezra Furman and The Orb. Nothing plays until you press it. Behind my desk sits a bookshelf of the writers I return to again and again, among them Virginia Woolf, Emily Dickinson, Sylvia Plath, Deleuze and Guattari, Spinoza, Tyson Yunkaporta and Helen De Cruz. At the far end of the room there is a Glimmer Window that does not look out onto the field at all, and nobody is quite sure where it does look out, so you will have to open the shutters and see for yourself.

There is also a regulation nook, because every good library needs one, with a small mountain of blankets, a squad of squishmallows, the smell of vanilla cupcakes, a standing supply of coffee, and cheese and pesto for emergencies. The cats, the dog and the hamster who share the yurt with me all have strong opinions about who it really belongs to. By the door you will find pebbles, in the spirit of penguin pebbling: a basket of little things I have left out for anyone to take, and a bowl where you can leave one of your own. As everywhere on the street, the dial lets you choose how loud it gets, and at Max Glitter the fairy lights come on and the record starts to turn.

Visit my Faery Yurt

References

Morrison, G. (Writer), & Case, R. (Artist). (1990). Doom Patrol (Vol. 2). DC Comics.

Stimpunks Foundation. (2026). Stimpunks.World . https://stimpunks.world/

posts.title: cavendish space
posts.excerpt: Caves, campfires and watering holes: Cavendish Space is a Stimpunks and Autistic Realms collaboration on places built to fit neurodivergent bodyminds.
posts.text:
A collaboration between Helen Edgar of Autistic Realms and Ryan Boren, Stimpunks Foundation

We wanted to make something together that said, “There is a place here built to fit you, not the other way round.”

Cavendish Space is our name for a psychologically and sensorially safe space, one that makes room for flow, for rest, and for coming together on our own terms. It draws on three of the oldest patterns in human learning and relating: the cave, the campfire and the watering hole. Many of us who are neurodivergent need to move between all three to feel regulated and to be creative, and too many of the rooms we live, learn and work in only offer one of them.

Did you know?

The name comes from Henry Cavendish, the eighteenth-century natural philosopher who discovered hydrogen. Steve Silberman’s NeuroTribes tells the story of a man who was very likely Autistic, and who shaped his whole life around the spaces he needed (Silberman, 2015). He had his cave, a quiet sensory and social cocoon where he could think. He had a campfire in the small, familiar Monday Club of the Royal Society, where he could sit at the edge and join in when he chose. He reached the wider watering holes of science at a comfortable distance, through his friend Charles Blagden, who carried his ideas out into the world. One life held all three spaces, and the freedom to move between them made his work possible.

The three spaces themselves come from educator David Thornburg’s primordial learning metaphors, which describe the places humans have always gathered to learn, long before there were schools or offices (Thornburg, 2014). Ryan and I recognised them straight away. I spent twenty years in classrooms with children with profound and multiple learning disabilities, building sensory niches alongside them, and Ryan spent thirty years building creative teams in technology around the same rhythm of solitude and intermittent collaboration. We were both making Cavendish Space long before we had the language for it, and we dedicate the idea to the memory of Steve Silberman, a true ally to our community.

Where would you like to go today?

There is no right order and no wrong choice. You might need your cave this morning and a campfire by the evening, and that movement is part of how we stay regulated.

• 🪨 The Cave : solitude and sensory regulation. A place to be alone, rest, focus and withdraw safely, with full say over your own sensory world.

• 💧 The Watering Hole : social connection and co-regulation. A place to be near others without having to join in, for conversation and exchange, body doubling and neurodivergent love languages.

• 🔥 The Campfire : shared meaning and orientation. A small, familiar circle for storytelling, collective understanding and low-demand presence.

Head into Cavendish Space to show how you feel with the Cavendish Cards (no reading or explaining needed), set up a room so it can hold all of these zones, or read more about the ideas behind it. Everything there is free to use and share.

Step into Cavendish Space

References

Silberman, S. (2015). NeuroTribes: The legacy of autism and the future of neurodiversity . Avery.

Thornburg, D. (2014). From the campfire to the holodeck: Creating engaging and powerful 21st century learning environments . Jossey-Bass.

posts.excerpt: queering.earth A New Cabinet for Post-Normal Possibilities A collaboration between Helen Edgar and Ryan Boren, Stimpunks Foundation “Weird” comes from wyrd, Old English for fate and becoming. I used that etymology as the spine of a blog a while back, and it turns out it’s also the heart of something else and it has evolved […]
posts.text:
queering.earth

A New Cabinet for Post-Normal Possibilities

A collaboration between Helen Edgar and Ryan Boren, Stimpunks Foundation

“Weird” comes from wyrd, Old English for fate and becoming. I used that etymology as the spine of a blog a while back, and it turns out it’s also the heart of something else and it has evolved into queering.earth

queering.earth

is alive

Starstuff.earth worked from physics: atoms forged inside stars, nothing existing in isolation, we shared the message of everything living and non-living belongs here all the way down to our star stuff.

queering.earth works from the humanities instead and what has been handed to us.

We are using neuroqueering a a verb, subverting neuronormativity and heteronormativity at the same time, because the two were never really separate arguments to begin with.

We have been queering readings of literature, poetry, art, people and history, and are excited to add more to our cabinet of curiosities.

Every sheet gets mounted and accessioned the way a herbarium mounts a pressed plant, and every correction we’ve had to make lives in a register anyone read as we want to be transparent and not hide flaws or changes of thought and lack of knowledge.

We are queering the design, text and fonts but you can switch the decorative typography off if it gets in your way to plain text as we want everything accessible.

This isn’t really a launch, it’s closer to perhaps catching us mid-sentence, as we pause to reflect on what we have been doing so far.

There’s more coming.

Come and explore what we have so far at queering.earth

See you on the queerside !

posts.title: star stuff
posts.excerpt: Every atom in you was forged inside a star. Explore Star Stuff — a collaboration on cosmology, Deleuzian philosophy, and neurodivergent belonging.
posts.text:
A collaboration between Helen Edgar and Ryan Boren, Stimpunks Foundation

We wanted to make something together that said, ” You belong here, all the way down to your star stuff”!

Did you know?

Every atom heavier than hydrogen was forged inside a star. The calcium in your bones, the iron in your blood, the oxygen you’re breathing right now — all of it lived inside a star before it became part of you (Sagan, 1980). We share around 97% of the same atoms as the galaxy itself (Howell, 2017). Not a metaphor. It’s who we are.

For those of us who’ve spent a lifetime being told we’re too much, not enough, or wrong somehow, we may feel this intensely. The universe didn’t create a single correct configuration of matter and call everything else a mistake. It made diversity — endless variation, always becoming, always connecting, always transforming.

We are all part of the same galaxy: connecting, interconnecting, interdependent.

This project grew out of conversations between myself and Ryan, and it weaves together several threads that don’t often get to sit together: quantum physics, Deleuzian philosophy, and Autistic experiences.

Relational quantum mechanics tells us that nothing exists in isolation — that what something is only makes sense in relation to everything around it.

Deleuze gives us difference-before-identity: the idea that variation comes first, and sameness is the thing that had to be built. Held together, they offer a different starting point for thinking about neurodivergence — not as a deviation from a baseline, but as difference that was there from the beginning, the way stars were never one kind of star.

It’s become a shared home across two spaces: a reflection here on More Realms, and a whole constellation of writing, zines, and art over at Stimpunks.

Come and Explore:

• 🌌 Read the full Star Stuff page — the heart of the project: the manifesto, the science, the philosophy, and reflections from the community, all together at Stimpunks

• 📖 Read the zines — eleven of them so far, including my own guest zine, Why Difference Comes First , which follows the quantum and Deleuzian thread in full, alongside community favourites like Bone Song and Underground

• ✨ Wander the Field Guides — neurodivergent constellations, the elements you’re made of, and the life forms that thrive in places we once thought impossible

• 🎧 Listen along — a 26-track playlist that carries the same spirit in sound
